chunks: How components are soldered on PCBs. The question: How are components soldered on a PCB?
Solder is a metal that melts at a low temperature and then freezes into a solid joint between a part and the board.
Which method you use depends on the part and on how many boards you build. Surface-mount parts are usually soldered by melting printed paste in an oven.
Through-hole parts are soldered by a wave of molten solder, a small moving nozzle, or by hand.
Think of making a tray of nachos. You lay down the cheese, set the chips on it, then bake the tray so the cheese melts and holds everything when it cools.
Reflow soldering works the same way, with solder paste as the cheese. If you bake a second side, the first side's cheese melts again.
Light chips stay put, but a heavy one could fall off.
Choose the process from the part type and volume. Reflow handles SMT; through-hole splits by quantity and by whether the bottom side is wave-compatible.
Solder: a metal alloy that melts at a low temperature and joins parts to pads.
Flux: a cleaning agent in the paste that removes oxide (the dull film metal grows in air) so the solder sticks. Reflow: melting printed paste in an oven.
Wave soldering: passing the board underside over a flowing wave of molten solder. Selective soldering: a small nozzle that solders chosen through-hole joints one at a time.
A board has small chip parts on both sides and one tall connector with legs through holes. Print paste, place parts and reflow side 1.
Flip the board, print, place and reflow side 2.
During the second pass, side 1 melts again, but its light parts stay held by surface tension, the pull of the molten solder's surface.
So the heavy parts go on the side reflowed last, or get glued. Finally, solder the connector with a selective nozzle or by hand. That is the whole idea.
"SMT parts are soldered by reflow: paste is printed, parts are placed, and an oven melts it. Through-hole parts are soldered by wave, selective or hand soldering.
On a double-sided board you reflow one side, flip, and reflow the other, putting heavy parts on the last side or gluing them, because surface tension only holds light parts upside down.
On mixed boards I'd reflow the SMT first and then do selective soldering or pin-in-paste for the through-hole parts."
